newsitem.title: UK: Weather, export policy hit Europe grain prices.
newsitem.headline: Weather, export policy hit Europe grain prices.

text.p: Rain and tightening EU export policy combined to force European grains prices lower as this week drew to a close.
As it started to rain in the parched west, forecasters and farming analysts said the rain did look as though it might just be sustained enough to make a difference.
The imposition by the EU grains management committee on Thursday of a 15 ECU tax on wheat exports was designed to push prices on the domestic market down, and on Friday it had the desired effect.
With the grain export campaign drawing to an end, weather largely dominated grain trade in France this week.
French wheat, barley and maize prices rose earlier this week on mounting fears that a persisting dry spell might hit crop yields.
But on Friday grain prices were significantly lower, depressed by forecasts of a change in the weather pattern over the weekend and by news the EU slapped a tax on wheat exports.
Anxiously awaited rainfall hit western France on Friday morning and more rain was expected to bring thirsty crops some relief over the next four days, meterological services said.
News of the EU's tax on wheat exports contributed to wheat prices' weakness down, dealers said.
"That's over for the old crop. Weather is now the focus," one dealer said.
On Thursday the European Union, eager to protect domestic supplies in the face of drought fears and volatile prices, also rejected all bids to export free-market barley.
This put a dampener on barley prices that on Wednesday had hit a high of 890 francs for April-June delivery into Rouen.
Strong demand from the starch and animal feed industry helped maize prices earlier this week. But prices were down on Friday in sympathy with wheat.
News the EU agreed on Thursday an import quota for 500,000 tonnes of maize for Spain and of 150,000 tonnes of maize for Portugal was also adding pressure.

The EU export moves helped drive UK prices down, but the weather was the main factor. Early in the week, prices were forced up by increasing sentiment that the prolonged dry weather had done real damage to the crop, but then forecasts of rain, which turned out true on Friday, forced prices back.

The level of activity on the UK market was low all week. "Although we're competitive on old crop the business isn't there," one exporter said in mid week. And new crop UK wheat could not compete with the French alternative, he said.
On Thursday the absence of many market players as the trade headed for the Grain and Feed Trade Association's annual dinner in London helped stifle business.
German wheat markets were slow to react to the EU's new tax, traders said on Friday.
Leading staff responsible for strategy in a number of trade houses had not returned from London where the annual GAFTA dinner was held on Thursday.
"The EU move was not that surprising, given they already closed the wheat export season last week," one trader said.
"It will have a dampening effect on internal old crop prices, which will be enhanced by the fact that consumers are not forthcoming and that crop weather is improving."
Rye markets were quiet. Compound feed plants were looking for old crop barley, which supported prices.
Spanish grains prices were little changed from last week's levels, although maize came off slightly after news of EU approval for imports of U.S. maize on Thursday, dealers said.
Otherwise the market was very quiet with last week's rain still not affecting prices.
"Prices are still high, and everyone's waiting for farmers to come out and sell. But so far they haven't, perhaps because the rain hasn't been heavy enough," said a dealer in Barcelona.
Light rain forecast today in some northern and central regions, with moderate showers expected in the north over the weekend might see prices come down next week, he said.
